title: Derivation and application of a general scaling relation between the dc and asymptotic high-frequency optical Hall responses
authors: E. Abelev, R. Romero, N. P. Armitage
abstract: Based on the Kramers-Krong relations, we derive and apply a quite general expression that that relates the low frequency quasi-dc Hall conductivity to the asymptotic high frequency optical Hall response (and its manifestations in Kerr and Faraday effects) for time-reversal symmetry breaking (TRSB) states of matter like ferromagnets and time-reversal symmetry breaking superconductors as well as metals in magnetic field. Parametric plots shows this relation is obeyed exactly for the trivial single-mode case of sharp cyclotron resonance, and approximately for theoretical models for ferromagnets and TRSB superconductors. We also apply it to the experimental data from a variety of ferromagnetic systems and show reasonable agreement there as well. We use the relation to predict, from the size of the spontaneous Kerr effect at the pseudogap temperature of the cuprate superconductors that cuprates should exhibit an anomalous Hall effect of approximately 0.1 Ohm$^{-1}\cdot$cm$^{-1}$. This is a small value, but one within experimental reach and we encourage the search for it. Although not explicitly quantum geometric, our treatment has some similarities to efforts to set bounds on physical quantities based on quantum geometric relations and limited physical information.
summary: This work establishes a general scaling relation linking the DC Hall conductivity to the high-frequency optical Hall response in time-reversal symmetry breaking systems. By applying this relationship, the authors make a quantitative prediction for the anomalous Hall effect in cuprate superconductors based on their measurable Kerr rotation signals.
main_problem: The paper derives a general scaling relation connecting the low-frequency (quasi-dc) Hall conductivity to the asymptotic high-frequency optical Hall response in Time-Reversal Symmetry Breaking (TRSB) materials.
main_result: A scaling relation, $	ext{Re}|\sigma_{xy}(\omega)| \propto |\sigma_{xy}(0)| (\delta/\omega)^2$, is derived and shown to hold for several models. This is used to predict a measurable anomalous Hall effect in cuprate superconductors based on their Kerr effect measurements.
method: The derivation relies on the Kramers-Kronig relations, connecting $\sigma_{1,xy}(\omega 	o 0)$ to $\sigma_{1,xy}(\omega \gg 	ext{gap})$ by analyzing the frequency dependence of the optical conductivity in different limits.
model_or_system: The study applies to TRSB states like ferromagnets and superconductors (e.g., cuprates), modeled using concepts from cyclotron resonance, Dirac continua, and superconducting gap structures.
key_observables: Hall conductivity ($\sigma_{xy}$), Kerr effect signal ($	heta_K$), quasi-dc Hall conductivity ($\sigma_{1,xy}(\omega 	o 0)$), and high-frequency optical response ($\sigma_{1,xy}(\omega \gg 	ext{gap})$).
important_parameters: Characteristic energy scales like the superconducting gap ($2\Delta$) or cyclotron frequency ($\omega_c$); the ratio $\delta/\omega$.
main_assumptions: The derivation assumes specific functional forms for conductivity in high and low-frequency limits, and the application to cuprates relies on relating the Kerr effect magnitude to the DC Hall response.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the derivation using dirty limit TRSB superconductors (Fig. 1) and compare $\sigma_{1,xy}$ and $\sigma_{2,xy}$ for cyclotron resonance in Drude/Dirac models (Figs. 2 & 3).
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by deriving the general scaling relation using KK relations, testing it against idealized models (cyclotron resonance), validating it with theoretical TRSB models, and finally applying the derived relationship to predict a specific measurable quantity in cuprate superconductors.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful, universal diagnostic tool—a scaling law—to connect disparate measurements (DC vs. optical) in complex quantum materials exhibiting broken symmetries, which is relevant for understanding exotic electronic states.
